questions.title: How can a defendant challenge consent given by a co-occupant spouse under the Fourth Amendment?
questions.question_body: In United States v. Coleman (7th Cir. 2025), Coleman was convicted of unlawful firearm possession after firearms were found in his home. The officers entered based on consent given by his wife, Lisa, not by Coleman himself. The court cites United States v. Matlock for the principle that a third party with shared privacy interests can consent to a search. I'm confused about the standing doctrine here. If Lisa had authority to consent to the entry, how does Coleman have standing to challenge that consent? And if both parties have equal privacy interests, does the consenting party's permission effectively waive the non-consenting party's Fourth Amendment rights? What are the limits of this third-party consent doctrine?

questions.title: Does an officer's statement that he 'needs' to enter a home render subsequent consent coerced under the Fourth Amendment?
questions.question_body: In the Coleman case, the officer said 'I'm sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure [the kids are okay],' and Lisa then said 'Okay.' Coleman argued that the word 'need' made the statement coercive because it implied the officer had a duty to enter, leaving Lisa no real choice. The court rejected this, finding the totality of circumstances showed voluntary consent. I'm struggling with where the line is between an officer expressing legitimate urgency about safety and an officer effectively asserting authority that overrides a person's free will. How do courts distinguish between persuasive language about safety concerns and coercive language that invalidates consent? Is there any precedent on magic words like 'need' versus 'would like to' in consent contexts?

questions.title: Does a prior refusal to consent make a later grant of consent more likely to be deemed voluntary?
questions.question_body: In Coleman, Lisa initially refused entry ('I'd prefer you not'), but later consented after the officer asked again in a different way. The court used her initial refusal as evidence that she understood she could say no and that her later consent was voluntary. But I've also read cases where repeated requests after a refusal are considered coercive—the idea being that badgering someone into compliance undermines voluntariness. Here, the officer only asked twice and the conversation lasted only a few minutes. Is there a framework for determining when re-asking for consent after a refusal crosses into coercion? Does the fact that the second request was phrased differently matter?

questions.title: What is the scope of consent when someone allows officers to enter to 'check on the kids'?
questions.question_body: In Coleman, Lisa consented to officers entering to check on her children's welfare. Once inside, the officers canvassed the entire home, located Coleman in a separate bedroom, conducted a protective pat-down, and questioned the children—all of which led to information used to secure a search warrant. Coleman argued the officers exceeded the scope of Lisa's consent. The court held that checking on the children's welfare 'necessarily required' scanning the home, locating everyone, and asking basic questions. This seems like a very broad reading of the scope of consent. How broadly do courts interpret the scope of consent to enter a home for a welfare check? Would the officers have been within scope if they opened closed doors, searched closets, or went into areas where the children clearly were not located?

questions.title: Why does the court apply 'clear error' review rather than de novo review to the voluntariness of consent?
questions.question_body: In Coleman, the Seventh Circuit says it reviews the district court's finding of voluntary consent for 'clear error.' I had understood voluntariness of consent to be a mixed question of law and fact, or at least that the legal question of whether facts amount to coercion should be reviewed de novo. The court treats this as a pure factual finding entitled to deference. When is clear error the appropriate standard for Fourth Amendment consent issues, and when should an appellate court conduct a fresh review? Does the existence of body camera footage change the analysis, since the appellate court can see exactly what happened?

questions.title: How does information obtained during a consensual entry relate to a subsequent search warrant?
questions.question_body: In Coleman, the officers entered the home based on Lisa's consent, then spoke to the children who told them Coleman had pointed a gun at their mother. The officers used this information to secure a search warrant, which led to the recovery of firearms. I'm confused about the relationship between the initial consensual entry and the later warrant. If the initial entry was consensual, does that mean any evidence observed during that entry is automatically admissible in the warrant application? Could Coleman argue that the children's statements were obtained as a result of the officers exceeding the scope of consent, and therefore the warrant was based on illegally obtained information (fruit of the poisonous tree)?

questions.title: Why did the court decline to address exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery as alternative grounds?
questions.question_body: At the end of the Coleman opinion, the court says that because it affirmed on consent grounds, it did not need to consider the government's alternative arguments based on exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery. I understand that courts generally avoid deciding issues when a case can be resolved on other grounds, but I'm wondering whether this creates problems for the government on remand or in future cases. If a higher court were to reverse the consent finding, would the government be able to raise these alternative theories at that point, or would they be considered waived? Also, what would the exigent circumstances argument have looked like here—a domestic violence call with threats involving a firearm?

questions.title: How does a conditional guilty plea with reserved appeal rights work procedurally?
questions.question_body: In Coleman, the defendant 'chose to plead guilty while reserving his right on appeal to challenge the suppression ruling.' I want to understand the procedural mechanics of this. Under what rule or statute is a defendant allowed to plead guilty but still appeal a pretrial motion denial? Does the plea agreement have to specify which issues are reserved? If the Seventh Circuit had reversed the suppression ruling, would the conviction be vacated entirely, or would the case just be remanded for further proceedings? And why would a defendant choose this route rather than going to trial and then appealing the suppression ruling if convicted?
